newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Assembly vote may pave way for tobacco suit.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Assembly vote may pave way for tobacco suit.

text.p: California's state Assembly on Thursday approved a bill that would clear the way for the state to sue tobacco companies to recoup public health care costs related to smoking.
The bill, by Assembly Speaker Cruz Bustamante, passed 59-11 and now advances to the state Senate.

"This bill removes any real or claimed legal barrier to the attorney general filing suit against tobacco companies to recover state paid medical costs of treating smokers," Bustamante, a Democrat, said.
An opponent of the bill, Republican Assemblyman Brett Granlund, argued the state collects more in taxes from smokers than it spends to treat them for smoking-related illnesses.

California, the most populous state with potentially billions of dollars in claims, has so far not sued major tobacco companies. But pressure has been building on state lawmakers in recent months to join the legal battle.

Liggett Group, owned by Bennett LeBow's Brooke Group Ltd., broke ranks with other tobacco companies in March by agreeing to settle with 22 state attorneys general who sued the industry to recoup smoking-related health care costs.

Bustamante said his legislation, introduced in response to the Liggett accord, would clarify an existing product liability law, removing any barriers that prevent Republican state Attorney General Dan Lungren from joining product liability lawsuits against tobacco companies.
Lungren has long maintained that state litigation would likely fail because of a controversial 1987 state law shielding tobacco companies from product liability claims.
In recent weeks, Lungren has said California would likely join other states in suing the major tobacco companies if the state legislature removes the legal barriers.
Bustamante's urgency legislation would, if approved by the Senate and signed by Republican Gov. Pete Wilson, take effect immediately. Democrats control both houses of the legislature.
A similar bill by Senator Quentin Kopp, an Independent, was approved by the state Senate last week. The Kopp bill is not urgency legislation and would not take effect until 1998.
Lawmakers said both bills could be passed by the legislature and sent to the governor for his signature.
